name: Vegetarian and pescatarian diets
lead: Vegetarian diets exclude meat, and pescatarian diets exclude meat but include fish and seafood; both may include eggs and dairy. The term pescetarian was coined in the UK in the late 1980s and about 3 percent of adults worldwide were estimated to follow this diet in 2017-2018.[11] They are discussed in looksmaxxing contexts as reduced-meat options for skin, leanness and general health.

Research is mostly observational. A UK Biobank cohort and meta-analysis examined meat, vegetarian, pescatarian and fish-poultry diets and cancer risk, a Swiss population study linked these diets to cardiovascular risk factors, and studies of young people compared micronutrient status.[1][2][4][10]
infobox: Fish and seafood, sometimes eggs and dairy

paras: Lacto-ovo vegetarians eat dairy and eggs; lacto vegetarians eat dairy only; ovo vegetarians eat eggs only; vegans eat no animal products; flexitarians eat mostly plants with occasional meat or fish.[11] Pescatarian diets are close to Mediterranean-style eating, which features fish and plants.[11]

In the UK Biobank analysis of 409,110 participants, researchers compared diet types with all-cancer and site-specific cancer incidence, and combined the results with a meta-analysis of prospective cohorts.[1] The Swiss study examined prevalence, sociodemographic features and cardiovascular risk factors among vegetarian, pescatarian and flexitarian dieters.[2]

Studies of Norwegian and Swedish 16-24-year-olds compared micronutrient intake and status, and food groups and biomarkers, across vegan, lacto-ovo-vegetarian, pescatarian and omnivorous diets.[4][8][10] A study of Americans found popular diets differ in carbon footprint and diet quality.[3] Other studies cover nutritional status and habits, thrombotic risk factors and erectile function with organic and fasting regimens.[5][6][7] Modelling research examined diets with reduced animal protein.[9]
Wikipedia notes that some fish contain mercury and PCBs, and that choosing low-mercury fish reduces exposure.[11]

The studies identified are observational or cross-sectional, covering cancer, cardiovascular risk factors, micronutrient status and diet quality.[1][2][4][5][8][10] No clinical trials were found testing vegetarian or pescatarian diets for skin or facial appearance.
No substantial forum discussion specific to these diets was identified; they appear as moderate options between omnivorous and vegan eating.

card.summary: Reduced-meat diets with decent population data on health but nothing on looks.
card.note: Some fish contain mercury; vegetarians should watch B12 and iron.

quick.overview:
Vegetarian diets exclude meat; pescatarian diets add fish and seafood. Both are common, moderate alternatives to omnivorous or vegan eating.

Studies are observational and focus on cancer, cardiovascular risk and nutrient status; none test appearance.
quick.mechanism: They shift intake toward plants and, for pescatarians, fish-derived omega-3. Any effect on skin or leanness is untested.
quick.risks: Nutrient status studies compare B12, iron and others across diets; some fish carry mercury and PCBs.
